excerpt: Share Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Mail Two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who says they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight. The agent can read the file and send email, so it fulfills the user request. Semantic governance policies, available in Preview in Gemini platform, enable enterprises to govern their agents and provide guardrails to stop that call before it runs. They check each tool call an agent proposes against what the user asked for and against rules you write in plain language. Permissions alone can't catch this. They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules. A model can also be talked out of the rules in its system instructions, by a user with a good reason, or by a document telling it to do something nobody asked for, a technique called indirect prompt injection. So the check has to sit outside the agent. Semantic governance policies are enforced through a policy enforcement point, such as Agent Gateway , alongside the agent governance controls we expanded in October , so policies stay separate from your agent's code. Two checks before an action runs Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things: Your rules, in plain language. You write policies the way your legal or compliance team already writes rules, such as "Before the earnings release, quarterly results may be shared only with @example.com addresses." What the user asked for. This check ensures the proposed tool call has not deviated from the original user intent. This is on by default to protect against hijacking. A call has to pass both checks to run. Today, the policy enforcement point that Semantic governance policies support is Agent Gateway. You need to configure your agent so all your agent egress traffic goes through Agent Gateway, facilitating traffic between your agent and its model. y Data Privacy Stack Presidio (Origin from Latin praesidium ‘protection, garrison’) helps to ensure sensitive data is properly managed and governed. It provides fast identification and anonymization modules for private entities in text and images such as credit card numbers, names, locations, social security numbers, bitcoin wallets, US phone numbers, financial data and more. Project transition update Presidio has transitioned to a community-owned project. Read the full announcement here . Goals Allow organizations to preserve privacy in a simpler way by democratizing de-identification technologies and introducing transparency in decisions. Embrace extensibility and customizability to a specific business need. Facilitate both fully automated and semi-automated PII de-identification flows on multiple platforms. How it works Main features Predefined or custom PII recognizers leveraging Named Entity Recognition , regular expressions , rule based logic and checksum with relevant context in multiple languages. Options for connecting to external PII detection models. Multiple usage options, from Python or PySpark workloads through Docker to Kubernetes . Customizability in PII identification and anonymization. Module for redacting PII text in images . Warning Presidio can help identify sensitive/PII data in un/structured text. However, because it is using automated detection mechanisms, there is no guarantee that Presidio will find all sensitive information. Consequently, additional systems and protections should be employed. Demo Link to demo: https://huggingface.co/spaces/presidio/presidio_demo Presidio's modules Presidio analyzer : PII identification in text Presidio anonymizer : De-identify detected PII entities using different operators Presidio image redactor : Redact PI
